Password and Authentication Management Policy

Purpose
This policy establishes minimum standards for password creation, storage, reset, and authentication controls across company-managed systems. Because the company handles customer personal data, order information, and payment-related workflows, strong authentication practices are required to reduce the risk of unauthorized access and operational disruption.

Scope
This policy applies to all employees, contractors, temporary workers, service accounts, and third parties who access company systems. It covers workstations, cloud applications, VPN, internal admin tools, ticketing platforms, warehouse systems, and any environment containing production, staging, or sensitive business data.

Password Requirements
User passwords must be at least 14 characters long and must not contain easily guessed words such as the company name, season plus year, keyboard patterns, or reused personal passwords. Passphrases are strongly preferred over short complex strings because they are easier to remember and harder to guess. Passwords may not be shared, emailed in plain text, stored in unsecured notes, or reused across company and personal systems. Systems that support it must screen new passwords against common breach or weak-password lists.

Multi-Factor Authentication
Multi-factor authentication is required for email, VPN, identity provider accounts, administrator access, finance systems, customer data platforms, and any externally accessible internal tool. Approved second factors include authenticator apps, hardware security keys, or other centrally approved methods. SMS should only be used where no stronger option is available and must be phased out for privileged accounts.

Password Managers and Storage
Employees must use the company-approved password manager for storing unique credentials. Shared credentials should be avoided whenever technically possible. When a shared secret is unavoidable, it must be stored in a centrally managed shared vault with defined owners and periodic review. Local browser storage for privileged passwords is prohibited unless managed by IT policy and encryption controls.

Reset and Recovery
Self-service password reset may be used only through approved identity workflows. Help desk staff must verify user identity before assisting with resets and must not request the user's current password. Privileged account resets require additional verification and must be logged. If there is any sign that an account has been compromised, IT must force a credential reset, revoke active sessions, and review recent authentication activity before restoring normal access.

Service Accounts and Rotation
Service accounts must have named business owners, limited permissions, and rotation schedules documented by IT. Where supported, service-to-service authentication should use keys, certificates, or managed identities instead of static passwords. Break-glass administrative credentials must be tightly controlled, sealed in an approved vault, and reviewed after every use.

Compliance and Enforcement
IT Security reviews authentication control adherence through periodic audits, access reviews, and incident investigations. Failure to follow this policy may lead to access suspension, corrective action, or vendor remediation requirements. Exceptions must be documented, time-bound, and approved by IT Security leadership.

User Awareness
All workforce members must complete annual security awareness training covering password hygiene, phishing resistance, MFA use, and credential reporting expectations. Repeated risky behavior may require targeted retraining or temporary access restrictions.

Credential Reporting
Users must report suspected credential exposure immediately so IT can reset access, review login activity, and determine whether broader containment steps are required.
